name: Yoke
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only classification notes (Jones 1987, Donohue 1999) and sociolinguistic survey (Clouse & Ma 2002); no phonology located

sources.citation: Reesink, Ger & Michael Dunn. 2012. Systematic typological comparison as a tool for investigating language history. Language Documentation & Conservation Special Publication 5, 38 pp.
sources.note: Typological-feature paper (features include 'weight sensitive stress' / 'syllable position stress' for its sample) but Yoke and Pauwi do not occur anywhere in the text; irrelevant.

Consonant and vowel tables copied from Clouse, Donohue & Ma 2002 ('On the surface, at least, Yoke has the following sounds'); no mention of stress. Cites Clouse et al. 2002, Reesink & Dunn 2018 and the Donohue 1998 NUS page.

sources.citation: Clouse, Duane, Mark Donohue & Felix Ma. 2002. Survey report of the north coast of Irian Jaya. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2002-078. 10 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 4.2 Yoke (p. 8) gives only a chart of 'apparent surface phonemes' (p t k / b d g / v r gh / m n ny / w s y; i e a o u) and morphosyntax; nothing on stress for Yoke. The only stress remark (p. 9, 'some instances of a stressed schwa') concerns Airoran/Samarokena.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1999 (ms., Sentani, May 1999). Warembori: annotated grammar sketch (un-annotated version published as Donohue 1999, Warembori, Languages of the World/Materials 341, Muenchen: Lincom Europa). 76 pp.; sec. 15.2 'Comparison with Yoke', pp. 58-61.
sources.note: Stress is described only for Warembori (sec. 2.2, p. 7: 'Stress is normally assigned to the penultimate syllable of a word or compound', with exceptions for nasal-final roots, identical vowels and 'heavy' consonants). The Yoke section (15.2, p. 58) says only 'Phonologically the languages are similar on a gross level' and then compares fricative contrasts, cognates and verbal affixes; no statement on Yoke stress.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1998. Lower Mamberamo: Warembori, and the Lower Mamberamo family (web page, National University of Singapore; sec. 2 'Yoke').
sources.note: Sociolinguistic and classificatory notes on Yoke (33% cognate with Warembori, Pauwi identification); no phonology and no stress.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1999. Warembori. Languages of the World/Materials 341. Muenchen: Lincom Europa.
